2008-Traditional Reading-2-1.article:
It used to be so straightforward . A team of researchers working together in the laboratory would submit the results of their research to a journal . A journal editor would then remove the authors ’ names and affiliations from the paper and send it to their peers for review . Depending on the comments received, the editor would accept the paper for publication or decline it . Copyright rested with the journal publisher , and researchers seeking knowledge of the results would have to subscribe to the journal .

No longer . The Internet — and pressure from funding agencies , who are questioning why commercial publishers are making money from government-funded research by restricting access to it — is making free access to scientific results a reality . The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development ( OECD ) has just issued a report describing the far-reaching consequences of this . The report , by John Houghton of Victoria University in Australia and Graham Vickery of the OECD , makes heavy reading for publishers who have , so far , made handsome profits . But it goes further than that . It signals a change in what has , until now , been a key element of scientific endeavor .

The value of knowledge and the return on the public investment in research depends , in part , upon wide distribution and ready access . It is big business . In America , the core scientific publishing market is estimated at between $7 billion and $11 billion . The International Association of Scientific , Technical and Medical Publishers says that there are more than 2,000 publishers worldwide specializing in these subjects . They publish more than 1.2 million articles each year in some 16,000 journals .

This is now changing . According to the OECD report , some 75% of scholarly journals are now online . Entirely new business models are emerging ; three main ones were identified by the report ’s authors . There is the so-called big deal , where institutional subscribers pay for access to a collection of online journal titles through site-licensing agreements . There is open-access publishing , typically supported by asking the author ( or his employer ) to pay for the paper to be published . Finally , there are open-access archives , where organizations such as universities or international laboratories support institutional repositories . Other models exist that are hybrids of these three , such as delayed open-access , where journals allow only subscribers to read a paper for the first six months , before making it freely available to everyone who wishes to see it . All this could change the traditional form of the peer-review process , at least for the publication of papers .

Genetically speaking , there are advantages to avoiding substantial height . During childbirth , larger babies have more difficulty passing through the birth canal . Moreover , even though humans have been upright for millions of years , our feet and back continue to struggle with bipedal posture and cannot easily withstand repeated strain imposed by oversize limbs . “ There are some real constraints that are set by the genetic architecture of the individual organism ,” says anthropologist William Leonard of Northwestern University .

Genetic maximums can change , but don’t expect this to happen soon . Claire C. Gordon , senior anthropologist at the Army Research Center in Natick, Mass , ensures that 90 percent of the uniforms and workstations fit recruits without alteration . 2008-Traditional Reading-3-5.article:
In the early 1960s Wilt Chamberlain was one of the only three players in the National Basketball Association (NBA) listed at over seven feet . If he had played last season , however , he would have been one of 42 . The bodies playing major professional sports have changed dramatically over the years , and managers have been more than willing to adjust team uniforms to fit the growing numbers of bigger , longer frames .

The trend in sports , though , may be obscuring an unrecognized reality : Americans have generally stopped growing . Though typically about two inches taller now than 140 years ago , today ’s people — especially those born to families who have lived in the U.S. for many generations — apparently reached their limit in the early 1960s . And they aren’t likely to get any taller . “ In the general population today , at this genetic , environmental level , we’ve pretty much gone as far as we can go ,” says anthropologist William Cameron Chumlea of Wright State University . In the case of NBA players , their increase in height appears to result from the increasingly common practice of recruiting players from all over the world .

Growth , which rarely continues beyond the age of 20 , demands calories and nutrients — notably , protein — to feed expanding tissues . At the start of the 20th century , under-nutrition and childhood infections got in the way . But as diet and health improved , children and adolescents have , on average , increased in height by about an inch and a half every 20 years , a pattern known as the secular trend in height . Yet according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , average height — 5′9″ for men , 5′4″ for women — hasn’t really changed since 1960 .

Genetically speaking , there are advantages to avoiding substantial height . During childbirth , larger babies have more difficulty passing through the birth canal . Moreover , even though humans have been upright for millions of years , our feet and back continue to struggle with bipedal posture and cannot easily withstand repeated strain imposed by oversize limbs . “ There are some real constraints that are set by the genetic architecture of the individual organism ,” says anthropologist William Leonard of Northwestern University .

Genetic maximums can change , but don’t expect this to happen soon . Claire C. Gordon , senior anthropologist at the Army Research Center in Natick, Mass , ensures that 90 percent of the uniforms and workstations fit recruits without alteration . She says that , unlike those for basketball , the length of military uniforms has not changed for some time . And if you need to predict human height in the near future to design a piece of equipment , Gordon says that by and large , “ you could use today ’s data and feel fairly confident .”

2008-Traditional Reading-4-1.article:
In 1784 , five years before he became president of the United States , George Washington , 52 , was nearly toothless . So he hired a dentist to transplant nine teeth into his jaw — having extracted them from the mouths of his slaves .

That’s a far different image from the cherry-tree-chopping George most people remember from their history books . But recently , many historians have begun to focus on the role slavery played in the lives of the founding generation . They have been spurred in part by DNA evidence made available in 1998 , which almost certainly proved Thomas Jefferson had fathered at least one child with his slave Sally Hemings . And only over the past 30 years have scholars examined history from the bottom up . Works of several historians reveal the moral compromises made by the nation ’s early leaders and the fragile nature of the country ’s infancy . More significantly , they argue that many of the Founding Fathers knew slavery was wrong — and yet most did little to fight it .

More than anything , the historians say , the founders were hampered by the culture of their time . While Washington and Jefferson privately expressed distaste for slavery , they also understood that it was part of the political and economic bedrock of the country they helped to create .

For one thing , the South could not afford to part with its slaves . Owning slaves was “ like having a large bank account ,” says Wiencek , author of An Imperfect God : George Washington , His Slaves , and the Creation of America . The southern states would not have signed the Constitution without protections for the “ peculiar institution ,” including a clause that counted a slave as three fifths of a man for purposes of congressional representation .

And the statesmen ’s political lives depended on slavery . The three-fifths formula handed Jefferson his narrow victory in the presidential election of 1800 by inflating the votes of the southern states in the Electoral College . Once in office , Jefferson extended slavery with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 ; the new land was carved into 13 states , including three slave states .

Still , Jefferson freed Hemings ’s children — though not Hemings herself or his approximately 150 other slaves . Washington , who had begun to believe that all men were created equal after observing the bravery of the black soldiers during the Revolutionary War , overcame the strong opposition of his relatives to grant his slaves their freedom in his will . Only a decade earlier , such an act would have required legislative approval in Virginia .

【选项概览】

A. show the primitive medical practice in the past

    说明过去医疗水平低下

B. demonstrate the cruelty of slavery in his days

    说明华盛顿时代奴隶制度的残酷

C. stress the role of slaves in the U.S. history

    强调奴隶在美国历史上的作用

D. reveal some unknown aspect of his life

    揭示华盛顿生活中不为人知的一面


【定位及答案】

在新闻文体中，文章开头的例证是用来引出话题的。第一段为例证本身，介绍了华盛顿曾让牙医把奴隶的牙齿镶到自已嘴里的轶事，从而考引出2段1句：他的这个形象和人们从历史书上记住的砍樱桃树的形象大不相同，即牙科手术旨在揭示华盛顿不为人知的另一种形象。D选项与此意思相符，故正确。


【错选分析】

【词汇干扰】A 说明过去医疗水平低下：利用1段2句中的dentist, transplant等医疗相关词汇设置干扰，医疗只是例证中涉及的内容，而非其目的，故排除。

【无中生有】B 说明华盛顿时代奴隶制度的残酷：文中未提及华盛顿时代奴隶制度是否残酷，故排除。

【偷换概念】C 强调奴隶在美国历史上的作用：选项利用2段2句设置干扰，选项中的stress 虽与2句中focus on语义相当，但前者的逻维主语是作者，后者的主语是many historians；此外，从华盛顿的牙科手术只能看出奴隶对他本人的作用，无法推出奴隶在美国历史上的作用。
2008-Traditional Reading-4-1.tips:
这道题的关键在于搞清楚作者开头讲那个“华盛顿用奴隶牙齿做牙科手术”的故事，到底是为了什么目的。很多同学一看到“牙医”“移植牙齿”这些词，就以为是在说以前医疗技术落后，其实这是个陷阱。

我们得往后看——第二段第一句马上就说：“这和我们从小在历史书里读到的那个诚实砍樱桃树的华盛顿完全不同。” 这句话就是题眼！作者不是要讨论医学、也不是专门批判奴隶制，而是想告诉我们：原来华盛顿还有这样一面，是我们以前不知道的。

所以，这个例子的作用是引出一个“反常识”的华盛顿形象，打破大家固有的印象。选项D说“揭示他生活中不为人知的一面”，正好对应这个意思。

至于其他选项：A项说“过去医疗原始”，虽然提到了牙医，但那只是故事的细节，不是作者的写作目的；B项强调“奴隶制的残酷”，文章确实涉及了奴隶，但重点不在批判制度本身；C项说“强调奴隶在美国历史中的作用”，那就更偏了，全文焦点始终是华盛顿，不是奴隶群体。

记住：考研阅读里，开头的故事或例子往往是为了引出主题或制造反差，别被细节带跑偏了。抓住后文的总结句，才能找准作者真正想表达的意思。

A. DNA technology has been widely applied to history research

这道题的关键在于准确理解第二段最后一句话的意思。原文提到“the fragile nature of the country’s infancy”，意思是美国在刚建国那会儿，国家还非常脆弱、不稳定。选项B说“在建国初期，美国面临许多微妙的形势”，这里的“建国初期”正好对应“infancy”，而“微妙的形势”也很好地表达了“fragile nature”所暗示的那种敏感、容易出问题的状态。所以B选项是对原文意思的合理转述。

比如，文章提到杰斐逊私下里明确表达过对奴隶制的反感，觉得这种制度在道德上站不住脚。但与此同时，他也清楚地知道，奴隶制深深嵌入了当时美国南方的政治和经济结构中，贸然废除可能引发严重后果。更复杂的是，他在担任总统后，实际上还扩大了奴隶制的地理范围——这和他的“反奴隶制”言论形成了鲜明对比。

因此，最准确的概括不是说他因为当了父亲就放人（B太片面），也不是说政治立场直接改变态度（A因果倒置），更不是聚焦于丑闻如何影响名声（D偏离主旨）。真正贴合全文信息的是：他对奴隶制的态度既矛盾又多面，不能用非黑即白来理解。所以正确答案是 C 选项——“他对奴隶制的态度是复杂的”。

2008-Traditional Reading-4-4.article:
In 1784 , five years before he became president of the United States , George Washington , 52 , was nearly toothless . So he hired a dentist to transplant nine teeth into his jaw — having extracted them from the mouths of his slaves .

That’s a far different image from the cherry-tree-chopping George most people remember from their history books . But recently , many historians have begun to focus on the role slavery played in the lives of the founding generation . They have been spurred in part by DNA evidence made available in 1998 , which almost certainly proved Thomas Jefferson had fathered at least one child with his slave Sally Hemings . And only over the past 30 years have scholars examined history from the bottom up . Works of several historians reveal the moral compromises made by the nation ’s early leaders and the fragile nature of the country ’s infancy . More significantly , they argue that many of the Founding Fathers knew slavery was wrong — and yet most did little to fight it .

More than anything , the historians say , the founders were hampered by the culture of their time . While Washington and Jefferson privately expressed distaste for slavery , they also understood that it was part of the political and economic bedrock of the country they helped to create .

For one thing , the South could not afford to part with its slaves . Owning slaves was “ like having a large bank account ,” says Wiencek , author of An Imperfect God : George Washington , His Slaves , and the Creation of America . The southern states would not have signed the Constitution without protections for the “ peculiar institution ,” including a clause that counted a slave as three fifths of a man for purposes of congressional representation .

And the statesmen ’s political lives depended on slavery . The three-fifths formula handed Jefferson his narrow victory in the presidential election of 1800 by inflating the votes of the southern states in the Electoral College . Once in office , Jefferson extended slavery with the Louisiana Purchase in 1803 ; the new land was carved into 13 states , including three slave states .

Still , Jefferson freed Hemings ’s children — though not Hemings herself or his approximately 150 other slaves . Washington , who had begun to believe that all men were created equal after observing the bravery of the black soldiers during the Revolutionary War , overcame the strong opposition of his relatives to grant his slaves their freedom in his will . Only a decade earlier , such an act would have required legislative approval in Virginia .
2008-Traditional Reading-4-4.analysis:
【选项概览】

A. Some Founding Fathers benefit politically from slavery.

    有些开国元勋在政治方面从奴隶制中受益

B. Slaves in the old days did not have the right to vote.

    在过去奴隶没有选举权

C. Slave owners usually had large savings accounts.

    奴隶主通常有巨额存款

D. Slavery was regarded as a peculiar institution.

    奴隶制被认为是一种特殊的制度


【定位及答案】

5段1句指出政治家（包括开国元勋）的政治前途依赖于奴隶制；5段2句则以杰斐逊在1800年大选中因五分之三计算式（每个奴隶可算作3/5人）险胜为例，力证了开国元勋能够从奴隶制中获得政治利益，因此A选项正确。


【错选分析】

【反向干扰】B 在过去奴隶没有选举权：4段3句提到在计算国会代表时，一个奴隶可算作3/5人，即其具有选举权，故排除。

【偷换概念】C 奴隶主通常有巨额存款：4段2句中的Owning slaves was“like having a large bank account”为比喻说法，奴隶主并非真的拥有巨额存款，故排除。

【以偏概全】D 奴隶制被认为是一种特殊的制度：4段3句提到南方各州要求对“特殊制度”，即奴隶制，予以保护，否则就不在宪法上签字。这只能说明南方各州认为奴隶制是特殊的，而非所有人都这么认为，故排除。
2008-Traditional Reading-4-4.tips:
这道题的关键在于回到原文第五段找线索。文章提到，当时一些政治人物——包括我们熟知的开国元勋——他们的政治前途其实和奴隶制紧密挂钩。紧接着举了一个特别具体的例子：托马斯·杰斐逊在1800年总统大选中，之所以能险胜对手，是因为宪法里那个“五分之三妥协”条款——也就是每个奴隶在人口统计中算作3/5个人，从而帮助南方州获得更多国会席位和选举人票。这个机制直接让拥有大量奴隶的州在政治上占了便宜，而作为南方代表的杰斐逊自然从中获益。

所以，选项A说“有些开国元勋在政治上从奴隶制中受益”，完全符合原文意思。这不是泛泛而谈，而是有明确史实支撑的结论。

再来看其他选项为什么不对。B选项说“奴隶过去没有投票权”，这话本身没错，但原文根本没提投票权的问题，属于常识正确但文中无依据，不能选。C选项讲奴隶主有“大额存款”，纯属无中生有，文章压根没讨论他们的银行账户。D选项提到“奴隶制被视为一种特殊制度”，虽然历史上确实有人用“peculiar institution”来形容奴隶制，但这个说法在本篇文章里并未出现，属于典型的“听起来熟悉但文中没说”的干扰项。

总结一下，做这类题千万别被“好像对”的选项迷惑，一定要问自己：这个信息原文真的说了吗？而且是直接支持题干的吗？ 只有紧扣文本、抓住具体例证，才能避开陷阱，选对答案。

【选项概览】

A. moral considerations

    道德考量

B. military experience

    从军经历

C. financial conditions

    经济条件

D. political stand

    政治立场


【定位及答案】

从题干中的Washington和e slaves定位在最后一段。该段❷句指出，华盛顿看到黑人在美国独立战争中的英勇表现后做出了解放奴隶的决定。可见，是战斗中的经历促使其做出了该决定，故B选项正确。


【错选分析】

【词汇干扰】根据上述分析，华盛顿解放奴隶的决定源于他的从军经历。A、C、D三个选项是分别利用文中的moral，economic，political等词设置的词汇干扰。
2008-Traditional Reading-4-5.tips:
这道题问的是华盛顿决定解放奴隶的主要原因是什么。我们要回到原文最后一段去找线索。文中提到，华盛顿在亲眼看到黑人士兵在美国独立战争中英勇作战之后，才下定决心要解放自己的奴隶。

注意这里的关键词是“看到黑人在战争中的表现”——这说明他的决定不是凭空产生的道德冲动，也不是因为缺钱或者政治压力，而是直接源于他在军队里的亲身经历。换句话说，正是那段军旅生涯、战场上的所见所闻，让他改变了对奴隶制的看法。

所以正确答案应该是B选项“从军经历”。其他几个选项虽然听起来好像也挺合理，比如A选项“道德考量”，但原文并没有说华盛顿是因为良心发现或者道德觉醒才这么做的；C选项“经济条件”和D选项“政治立场”在文中更是完全没提。题目考的就是你能不能抓住文章给出的具体因果关系，而不是靠自己的常识去脑补。

记住，考研阅读最忌“我觉得”，一定要“文章说”。只要紧扣原文细节，就能避开干扰项，选对答案。
